title: Squeeze Runs In Place
statement:
You get an array of characters chars. Shrink it by rewriting every run of the same character back to back:

  • A run of length 1 is written as just the character.
  • A longer run is written as the character followed by the run length in decimal, one digit per array slot. A run of 12 x's becomes "x", "1", "2".

Write the result into the front of chars itself, using only O(1) extra memory. The result is never longer than the input, so it always fits. Then return the written part, chars cut down to the new length k (the first k slots).

Only runs of neighbours count: the same letter appearing again later starts a new run.

examples.why: Three a's become a3, the single b stays b, two c's become c2.
A run of 12 writes two digit slots, '1' and '2', not one slot holding "12".
The two a's are not next to each other, so they are separate runs of length 1. Counting letters overall would wrongly give a2b.

constraints: chars[i] is a lowercase letter, uppercase letter, digit or symbol
hints: The written result never gets ahead of the part you are still reading. Why is that true?
Use a read index that scans a whole run and a write index where the squeezed form goes.
For each run: write the character at the write index, then, if the run is longer than 1, write each digit of its length. The read index jumps to the end of the run.

explain.intuition:
A run of length L takes L slots in the input and at most 1 + (number of digits of L) slots in the output. For L = 1 that is 1 slot, for L = 2 it is 2, and for larger L it is always fewer than L. So the writer never overtakes the reader, and you can safely write into the same array you are reading from.

That gives two indexes moving in the same direction: read runs ahead to measure each run, write trails behind and lays down the short form. It is the same read/write pattern as removing items from an array in place.
steps: While read < n: remember c = chars[read] and move read forward while it still sees c.
If the run length is more than 1, write each digit of the length, one per slot.
pitfalls: Writing the count as one slot like "12" instead of two slots "1", "2".
Writing "1" after single characters. Runs of length 1 get no number.
Counting total occurrences of each letter instead of runs of neighbours.

solutions.title: Build a new array
solutions.idea: Scan the runs and push the squeezed form into a fresh array. Easy to get right, but uses O(n) extra memory.

solutions.title: Read and write pointers in place
solutions.idea: The squeezed form of a run is never longer than the run, so a write pointer can trail a read pointer in the same array.

followups: Write the matching expand function. Which input becomes ambiguous if the characters themselves can be digits?
When does this encoding make data bigger, and how would you pick a different one for those inputs?
